title: Colder Than Their Own Blood
paragraphs: Seawater does not freeze at 0 degrees Celsius.
Its dissolved salts, about 35 grams per kilogram, push the freezing point down to roughly minus 1.9 degrees, and the coastal waters around Antarctica sit near that temperature for much of the year.
The blood of a typical marine bony fish is far less salty than the sea, about one third as concentrated, and freezes near minus 0.7 degrees.
A fish swimming in polar water is therefore colder than the freezing point of its own blood, a condition physicists call supercooling.
Supercooled liquid is stable only so long as nothing seeds it: a single ice crystal, touching the gills or swallowed with a mouthful of water, can freeze the whole fish.
That the danger is real was shown in the 1950s by the physiologist Per Scholander and his colleagues, who studied fish in a deep Labrador fjord.
Fish living at the bottom, in water below the freezing point of their blood, were supercooled and perfectly healthy, because no ice reached that depth to seed them.
Brought up and touched with a sliver of ice, the same fish froze at once.
Fish near the surface in winter, where ice was everywhere, had blood that froze at a lower temperature than the deep fish's, and their salts did not explain all of the difference.
Something else in the blood was lowering its freezing point, and no one yet knew what.
The answer came from the far end of the planet.
In the early 1960s Arthur DeVries, a Stanford graduate student, began working at McMurdo Station in Antarctica, where the water stays near minus 1.9 degrees all year and often holds ice.
Most fish there are notothenioids, a single group that dominates both the species and the biomass of the Antarctic shelf.
One of them, a small fish living directly under the sea ice, had blood that froze close to minus 2 degrees, and its salts explained only about half of that protection.

In 1969 DeVries and his adviser Donald Wohlschlag reported that when the serum was dialyzed, so that small molecules left through a membrane while large ones stayed behind, the extra freezing resistance stayed with the large molecules.
The agents were glycoproteins, proteins with sugars attached, and DeVries called them antifreeze glycoproteins.
Their structure is absurdly simple: the protein backbone is a short motif of three amino acids, alanine, alanine, threonine, repeated over and over, and a pair of sugars hangs from each threonine.
What they do is stranger than what they are.

Salt lowers the freezing point of water in proportion to the number of dissolved particles, an effect chemists call colligative, and by that rule the glycoproteins, which are present in modest numbers of relatively heavy molecules, should barely register.
Instead they lower the temperature at which the blood freezes hundreds of times more than their numbers would predict.
The clue to how lies in a quantity called thermal hysteresis.

Add a glycoprotein to water holding a small ice crystal and the temperature at which that crystal melts does not move; the temperature at which it grows drops by about a degree in the concentrations found in fish blood.
Between those two temperatures the crystal simply sits, neither growing nor shrinking, and that gap is the hysteresis.
The name antifreeze has always struck me as slightly misleading, and the hysteresis shows why.

The proteins do not prevent ice from forming the way salt on a winter road does; they prevent ice that already exists from getting any bigger, which for a fish that swallows the occasional crystal is the protection that matters.
In 1977 DeVries and James Raymond proposed the mechanism that, in its essentials, still stands.
The glycoproteins adsorb, or stick, to particular faces of a growing ice crystal and stay there.
Water can still join the crystal in the gaps between bound proteins, but only as a surface that bulges outward, and a sharply curved ice front must be colder before it can advance.
A crystal held this way looks like two six-sided pyramids joined at their bases.
When the temperature finally falls below the hysteresis point, the restraint fails all at once, and ice shoots out of the pyramids' tips as fine needles.
How a protein holds onto ice is a question the field answered once and then had to answer again.

The early picture was intuitive: hydroxyl groups on the threonines and sugars were thought to form hydrogen bonds with water molecules locked in the ice lattice, their spacing matching that of the lattice.

Later work, much of it from Peter Davies and his colleagues at Queen's University in Canada, found that the ice-binding face is flat and surprisingly water-repellent, and seems to order a layer of water into an ice-like arrangement that merges with the crystal.
The current account is more subtle than the first, and I suspect it is not the last.
Notothenioids are not the only fish with antifreeze, and the other solutions look nothing like theirs.

The winter flounder of the North American Atlantic coast makes a small, alanine-rich protein coiled into a single helix; the sea raven makes a globular protein resembling a sugar-binding lectin; the ocean pout makes a compact protein unlike either.
Each binds ice and produces hysteresis, and each is built on a different fold.
The surprise was the Arctic cod.
Arctic cods carry a glycoprotein nearly indistinguishable in composition from the notothenioid one: the same three-amino-acid repeat, the same pair of sugars on each threonine.
Were the two glycoproteins inherited from a shared ancestor?
In 1997 Liangbiao Chen, DeVries, and Chi-Hing Christina Cheng, all at the University of Illinois, answered no.

The notothenioid gene, they showed, had grown out of a gene for trypsinogen, a digestive enzyme precursor: it still carries pieces of the trypsinogen gene at both ends, while a nine-nucleotide stretch in between has been copied over and over to form the repeats.
Their molecular clock placed the gene's origin at roughly 5 to 14 million years ago, as the Southern Ocean cooled toward freezing.
The cod gene has no such pieces and no relation to trypsinogen, and later work from Cheng's laboratory traced it to DNA that had never coded for a protein.
Two lineages, starting from different raw material, had arrived at nearly the same molecule: convergent evolution at the level of a single protein.
The solution came with obligations.

The glycoproteins are small enough to be lost through an ordinary fish kidney, and most Antarctic notothenioids have kidneys without glomeruli, the filtering units that would otherwise strain the proteins into the urine.
Because marine fish drink seawater to replace water lost to their saltier surroundings, ice can enter by the gut as well, and the intestinal fluid carries antifreeze too.
There is a stranger cost.

In 2014 a team including Cheng and DeVries reported that fish from McMurdo Sound carried ice crystals inside their bodies, including the spleen, and that the proteins that keep those crystals from growing also keep them from melting, even slightly above their normal melting point.
Summer water never warms enough to clear them, so a fish may carry its ice for life.
I find that a sobering footnote to a story usually told as a triumph: the proteins are an arrangement with ice, not a victory over it.
The proteins have found work outside the fish.
One manufacturer uses a yeast-made version of the ocean pout protein to keep ice crystals small in ice cream, which gives low-fat varieties a smooth texture.
There are reasonable hopes for preserving transplant organs and frozen cells, where large crystals do the damage.
The promise of frost-proof crops, floated for decades, has delivered much less than advertised, and I would treat each new announcement in that line with patience rather than excitement.

What endures is the original observation: a graduate student on the ice, puzzled that fish lived in water colder than their blood should allow, found a protein that holds ice still, and six decades later it remains among the clearest examples of a molecule meeting a climate.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a marine bony fish swimming in polar seawater is described as supercooled because
choices: its blood holds roughly three times as much salt as the surrounding sea
the sea around it has begun to turn into ice
it is colder than the point at which its own blood freezes
ice crystals touch its gills with every mouthful of water it takes in
its blood, unlike seawater, freezes at exactly 0 degrees Celsius

proof.quote: colder than the freezing point of its own blood, a condition physicists call supercooling

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says a fish in polar water is colder than the freezing point of its own blood, and that this condition is what physicists call supercooling.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 1 says fish blood is about one third as concentrated as seawater, not three times saltier.
Not the definition: supercooling describes the fish's own state, and paragraph 1 treats ice in the water as the danger that seeds freezing.
Too strong: paragraph 1 says a single crystal can seed freezing, not that ice arrives with every mouthful.
Contradicted: paragraph 1 puts the freezing point of fish blood near minus 0.7 degrees; 0 degrees is the figure seawater is compared against.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the fish living at the bottom of the Labrador fjord survived in a supercooled state because
choices: their blood froze at a lower temperature than that of fish near the surface
no ice reached the depth at which they lived to seed them
the salts in their blood matched those of the sea
an unidentified substance in their blood lowered its freezing point
the water at the bottom of the fjord was warmer than their blood's freezing point

proof.quote: because no ice reached that depth to seed them

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says the bottom-dwelling fish were supercooled and healthy because no ice reached that depth to seed them; the danger was ice, not the cold itself.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 2 says it was the surface fish whose blood froze at the lower temperature.
Outside the passage: nothing says the deep fish had seawater-strength blood, and paragraph 1 says fish blood is far less salty.
Wrong fish: the unexplained extra protection belonged to the fish living near the surface in winter.
Contradicted: paragraph 2 says the deep fish lived in water below the freezing point of their blood.

questions.stem: The author ends paragraph 2 with the remark that 'no one yet knew what' primarily to
choices: cast doubt on the accuracy of Scholander's measurements
argue that salt alone explains a fish's resistance to freezing
suggest that the deep-water fish were not truly supercooled
set up the discovery described in the following paragraphs
explain why the surface fish froze more readily than the deep fish

proof.quote: Something else in the blood was lowering its freezing point, and no one yet knew what.
The answer came from the far end of the planet.

questions.why: Paragraph 2 closes on an open question, and paragraph 3 opens with the words 'The answer came from the far end of the planet.' The remark is a hinge: it names the mystery that DeVries's work will solve.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the author presents Scholander's results as reliable evidence that the danger is real.
Contradicted: the previous sentence says the salts did not explain all of the difference.
Contradicted: paragraph 2 says the deep fish were supercooled and perfectly healthy.
Reversed: the surface fish were the better protected ones; their blood froze at a lower temperature.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the 1969 report by DeVries and Wohlschlag showed that
choices: notothenioids make up most of the fish species on the Antarctic shelf
the blood of the fish beneath the ice froze at about minus 0.7 degrees
the small molecules that passed through the dialysis membrane carried the resistance
the freezing resistance stayed with the large molecules after dialysis
salts accounted for all of the blood's protection against freezing

proof.quote: the extra freezing resistance stayed with the large molecules

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says that when the serum was dialyzed, letting small molecules out through a membrane, the extra freezing resistance stayed with the large molecules; that is what the 1969 report showed.
distractorNotes: Wrong attribution: the dominance of notothenioids is background in paragraph 3, not a finding of the 1969 paper.
Wrong number: minus 0.7 degrees is the figure for a typical marine fish in paragraph 1; the Antarctic fish's blood froze close to minus 2.
Reversed: the small molecules left and the resistance stayed behind with the large ones.
Contradicted: paragraph 3 says the salts explained only about half of the protection.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the antifreeze glycoproteins of notothenioids are built from
choices: a single long helix rich in alanine with sugars attached at one end
a three-amino-acid motif, repeated, with a pair of sugars on each threonine
a globular protein that closely resembles a sugar-binding lectin
a chain of dissolved salts bound tightly to a protein backbone
a repeated motif of three sugars with a single amino acid attached to each one

proof.quote: a short motif of three amino acids, alanine, alanine, threonine, repeated over and over, and a pair of sugars hangs from each threonine

questions.why: Paragraph 4 describes the backbone as a short motif of three amino acids, alanine, alanine, threonine, repeated over and over, with a pair of sugars hanging from each threonine.
distractorNotes: Wrong fish: the alanine-rich single helix belongs to the winter flounder in paragraph 8.
Wrong fish: the lectin-like protein is the sea raven's, in paragraph 8.
Outside the passage: salts are dissolved in the blood, and nothing binds them to the protein.
Reversed: the repeat is three amino acids, and the sugars come as a pair on each threonine.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 4, the word 'register' most nearly means
choices: enroll on an official list of names
dissolve fully in the blood
show a feeling on one's face
be recorded by a measuring instrument
produce any noticeable effect

proof.quote: should barely register
Instead they lower the temperature at which the blood freezes hundreds of times more than their numbers would predict.

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says that by the colligative rule the few heavy glycoproteins should barely register, and the next sentence says that instead they lower the freezing point hundreds of times more than predicted. The word means to make a noticeable difference, not to enroll.
distractorNotes: This is the everyday meaning of the word, but no list or enrollment appears in the sentence.
Nothing in the sentence concerns whether the proteins dissolve; it concerns how much they change the freezing point.
A face registering emotion is another common use, but the sentence is about molecules in blood.
A gauge can register a reading, but the sentence is about the proteins' effect on the blood, not about any measurement.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if the glycoproteins worked only by the colligative rule, they would
choices: lower the freezing point of the blood far less than they actually do
have no effect whatsoever on the freezing point of the blood
hold an ice crystal between its melting and growth temperatures
lower the freezing point of the blood in strict proportion to their weight
force a growing ice crystal into a shape like two joined pyramids

proof.quote: by that rule the glycoproteins, which are present in modest numbers of relatively heavy molecules, should barely register
hundreds of times more than their numbers would predict

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says the colligative rule depends on the number of dissolved particles, that by that rule the few heavy glycoproteins should barely register, and that instead they do hundreds of times more. Take away the extra and only the small colligative share would remain.
distractorNotes: Too extreme: paragraph 4 says they should barely register under that rule, which is a small effect, not none.
Reversed: holding a crystal between two temperatures is the non-colligative behavior described in paragraph 5, not what the counting rule predicts.
Reversed: paragraph 4 says the colligative rule counts dissolved particles, not weight, and that the heavy molecules are too few to register.
Wrong mechanism: the pyramid shape in paragraph 6 comes from proteins sticking to crystal faces, not from the number of dissolved particles.

questions.stem: According to the passage, adding antifreeze glycoprotein to water that holds a small ice crystal
choices: lowers the temperatures at which the crystal melts and grows by equal amounts
raises the temperature at which the crystal melts by about a degree
lowers the growth temperature but not the melting point of the crystal
causes the crystal to shrink slowly until it disappears
lowers the melting point of the crystal while leaving its growth temperature alone

proof.quote: the temperature at which that crystal melts does not move; the temperature at which it grows drops

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says the temperature at which the crystal melts does not move, while the temperature at which it grows drops by about a degree at fish-blood concentrations. That one-sided shift is the thermal hysteresis.
distractorNotes: Half right: only the growth temperature falls; the melting point stays put.
Wrong direction: paragraph 5 says the melting point does not move at all.
Contradicted: paragraph 5 says the crystal sits between the two temperatures, neither growing nor shrinking.
Reversed: it is the growth temperature that drops and the melting point that stays fixed.

questions.stem: The author mentions salt on a winter road in paragraph 5 primarily to
choices: contrast what ordinary antifreeze does with what the proteins actually do
show that salt is a cheaper and more practical antifreeze than protein
explain why fish cannot simply raise the salt content of their blood
illustrate the colligative rule that was introduced in the previous paragraph
argue that the proteins deserve the name antifreeze after all

proof.quote: The proteins do not prevent ice from forming the way salt on a winter road does; they prevent ice that already exists from getting any bigger
The name antifreeze has always struck me as slightly misleading

questions.why: Paragraph 5 calls the name antifreeze slightly misleading and then explains: the proteins do not prevent ice from forming the way salt on a winter road does, they stop existing ice from growing. The road salt is the familiar case set against the fish's.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: no comparison of cost or practicality is made anywhere.
Outside the passage: the passage never discusses why fish do not raise their blood salt; the sentence is about how the proteins differ from salt.
Wrong purpose: the colligative rule belongs to paragraph 4, and this sentence is about preventing versus halting ice, not about counting particles.
Reversed: the author says the name is slightly misleading, and the road salt shows why.

questions.stem: A laboratory adds notothenioid antifreeze glycoprotein, at the concentration found in the fish's blood, to a tube of fresh water that contains one small ice crystal, and holds the tube at minus 0.5 degrees Celsius. Based on paragraph 5, the crystal would most likely
choices: melt away completely within a few minutes
grow slowly along the faces the proteins have not covered
remain the same size while it is held there
shoot out fine needles of ice from its tips
dissolve as the protein molecules bind to its faces

proof.quote: the temperature at which that crystal melts does not move; the temperature at which it grows drops by about a degree in the concentrations found in fish blood
Between those two temperatures the crystal simply sits, neither growing nor shrinking

questions.why: Paragraph 5 gives the rule: the melting point stays where it was, which for fresh water is 0 degrees, and the growth temperature drops by about a degree at fish-blood concentration, to about minus 1. Minus 0.5 falls in the gap, where the crystal simply sits, neither growing nor shrinking.
distractorNotes: Wrong side of the gap: the crystal would melt only above its unchanged melting point of 0 degrees.
Wrong side of the gap: growth needs a temperature below about minus 1, and paragraph 6 says the gaps are exactly where growth is held back.
Wrong temperature: paragraph 6 says the needles burst out only when the temperature falls below the hysteresis point.
Wrong mechanism: paragraph 6 says bound proteins stop growth; nothing says binding dissolves the crystal.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when the temperature falls below the hysteresis point, a crystal coated with antifreeze protein
choices: melts from the tips of its pyramids inward
sheds the proteins bound to its faces and stops growing
grows evenly on all faces at the same slow rate
shrinks until it reaches a size the proteins can hold
sends out fine needles of ice from its tips

proof.quote: ice shoots out of the pyramids' tips as fine needles

questions.why: Paragraph 6 ends by saying that when the temperature finally falls below the hysteresis point the restraint fails all at once, and ice shoots out of the pyramids' tips as fine needles.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the crystal grows, not melts, when the temperature falls.
Outside the passage: nothing says the proteins come off, and the crystal grows rather than stops.
Contradicted: paragraph 6 says the restraint fails all at once and growth comes as needles from the tips, not evenly.
Reversed: falling below the hysteresis point lets the crystal grow, not shrink.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the water-repellent character of the ice-binding face was 'surprising' because
choices: the earlier picture had the proteins bonding directly to water in the ice
the proteins had been thought to bind ice through their sugars alone
a flat surface was expected to slide off a crystal rather than stick to it
Davies and his colleagues had set out to confirm the earlier picture
the spacing of the proteins had been found not to match the ice lattice

proof.quote: were thought to form hydrogen bonds with water molecules locked in the ice lattice
flat and surprisingly water-repellent

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says the early picture had the hydroxyl groups forming hydrogen bonds with water molecules in the ice lattice. A face that bonds to water is the opposite of one that repels it, so a water-repellent face overturns that expectation.
distractorNotes: Half right: the early picture involved the hydroxyls on the threonines as well as the sugars, and it is the bonding to water that the new finding upset.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about flat surfaces sliding off crystals.
Outside the passage: the passage does not say what Davies's group set out to show.
Contradicted: the matching of spacing was part of the early picture, and the passage never says it failed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a fish that carries an antifreeze protein?
choices: winter flounder
sea raven
ocean pout
Arctic cod
herring

proof.quote: The winter flounder of the North American Atlantic coast makes a small, alanine-rich protein
the sea raven makes a globular protein
the ocean pout makes a compact protein
The surprise was the Arctic cod.

questions.why: Paragraph 8 names the winter flounder, the sea raven, and the ocean pout, and then introduces the Arctic cod. Herring appear nowhere in the passage.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 8 names the winter flounder and its alanine-rich helix.
Paragraph 8 names the sea raven and its lectin-like protein.
Paragraph 8 names the ocean pout, which returns in paragraph 11.
Paragraph 8 introduces the Arctic cod as the surprise, and paragraph 9 traces its gene.

questions.stem: According to the passage, all of the following were part of the 1997 findings of Chen, DeVries, and Cheng EXCEPT:
choices: The notothenioid gene grew out of a gene for trypsinogen.
The Arctic cod gene had grown out of a trypsinogen gene of its own.
A molecular clock placed the gene's origin at roughly 5 to 14 million years ago.
The antifreeze gene still carries pieces of the trypsinogen gene at both ends.
A short nine-nucleotide stretch had been copied over and over to form the repeats.

proof.quote: had grown out of a gene for trypsinogen
Their molecular clock placed the gene's origin at roughly 5 to 14 million years ago
still carries pieces of the trypsinogen gene at both ends
has been copied over and over to form the repeats
The cod gene has no such pieces and no relation to trypsinogen

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says the cod gene has no such pieces and no relation to trypsinogen; that is the whole point of the convergence story. The other four statements all appear in paragraph 9.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 9, sentence 3 says the notothenioid gene had grown out of a gene for trypsinogen.
Paragraph 9, sentence 4 gives the molecular clock estimate of roughly 5 to 14 million years.
Paragraph 9, sentence 3 says the gene still carries pieces of trypsinogen at both ends.
Paragraph 9, sentence 3 describes the nine-nucleotide stretch copied over and over.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a notothenioid whose kidneys had ordinary filtering units would most likely
choices: produce larger glycoproteins that the kidney could not strain out
take in less ice through its gut, since it would drink less seawater
accumulate more ice crystals in its spleen over its lifetime
lose part of its antifreeze into its urine and be less protected
have blood that froze at a lower temperature than other notothenioids

proof.quote: The glycoproteins are small enough to be lost through an ordinary fish kidney
the filtering units that would otherwise strain the proteins into the urine

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says the glycoproteins are small enough to be lost through an ordinary fish kidney, and that most notothenioids lack glomeruli, the filtering units that would otherwise strain the proteins into the urine. Give the fish those units back and the proteins would drain away.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: nothing suggests the fish could change the size of its proteins in response.
Unrelated: drinking in paragraph 10 is driven by water loss to the salty sea, not by the kidney.
Wrong link: the ice in the spleen in paragraph 10 is tied to the proteins preventing melting, not to kidney filtering.
Reversed: losing antifreeze would raise the temperature at which the blood freezes, not lower it.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward announcements of frost-proof crops is best described as
choices: hostile
cautious
enthusiastic
indifferent
amused

proof.quote: I would treat each new announcement in that line with patience rather than excitement
has delivered much less than advertised

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says the promise of frost-proof crops has delivered much less than advertised and that the author would treat each new announcement with patience rather than excitement. That is caution: not rejection, not enthusiasm.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the author counsels patience, not opposition.
Reversed: excitement is exactly what the author declines.
Too weak: the author cares enough to warn the reader and to weigh the record.
Wrong register: nothing in the sentence treats the announcements as funny.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Polar fishes survive in freezing water because their blood carries more salt than the sea around them
Antarctic and Arctic fishes inherited one antifreeze gene from a common ancestor that lived in cold seas
Antifreeze proteins have transformed food manufacturing and organ preservation
Proteins that hold ice still let polar fishes live below the freezing point of their own blood
Scientists still cannot explain how a protein can bind to the surface of a growing ice crystal

proof.quote: colder than the freezing point of its own blood
they prevent ice that already exists from getting any bigger
found a protein that holds ice still

questions.why: The passage opens with fish living below the freezing point of their own blood, spends its middle on how the glycoproteins keep existing ice from growing, and closes by calling that the enduring observation. The answer names both the problem and the solution; the others pick one detail or get it wrong.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 1 says fish blood is far less salty than the sea, and paragraph 3 says salts explain only about half of the protection.
Contradicted: paragraph 9 says the two glycoproteins arose independently from different raw material.
Too narrow: the applications occupy one paragraph, and the author is cautious about them.
Too strong: paragraph 7 says the binding question was answered, then revised, and may be revised again, not that it is unexplained.
